Let's begin with some practical dialogue examples and listening exercises.

data.heading: Dialogue Practice — Meeting Schedule
data.problem:
Complete the dialogue using appropriate articles:
A: When is meeting? B: They've changed date. It's on Tuesday now. — the meeting
(a specific, known meeting — also accepted a meeting in some keys); the date; — Tuesday.
steps: Identify the specific nouns requiring articles
Determine whether each noun needs 'a', 'an', 'the', or no article
Apply the rules for specific and general references
data.result:
Corrected dialogue:
A: When is the meeting? B: They've changed the date. It's on Tuesday now.

The task is to complete the dialogue using appropriate articles.

Then determine whether each noun needs 'a', 'an', 'the', or no article.
Finally, we apply the rules for specific and general references.
The corrected dialogue would be: 'A: When is the meeting? B: They've changed the date. It's on Tuesday now.'

Your task is to listen carefully to each speaker.
Identify whether each person agrees or disagrees with the statement.

data.heading: Generalizing Language
bullets: They aren't always very good at...

narr: This week introduces target language for generalizing.
These phrases help express general opinions or tendencies.
Generally speaking is used to introduce a broad statement.
In general serves a similar purpose to generally speaking.
On the whole indicates a conclusion after considering all factors.
They tend to suggests a common pattern or tendency.
They aren't always very good at highlights a common weakness or limitation.

data.heading: Discussion Practice — Using Generalizing Language
data.problem:
Work in groups of three. Take turns to talk about the statements. Use the language from the information box.
Statement list: Children shouldn't be allowed to use the internet by themselves until they are 12 years old. / Going to the cinema is much better than watching films on TV. / Working from home is more enjoyable than going to work. / Breakfast is the most important meal of the day. / It's important to exercise at least three times a week. / Being a teacher is the most stressful job in the world. / Cats make better pets than dogs, especially for older people. / Art and music are subjects that are not worth studying at university.
steps: Choose a statement from the list
Formulate your opinion using generalizing phrases
Provide supporting reasons for your position
Respond to others' viewpoints using appropriate language
data.result: Model answers: Generally speaking, I think going to the cinema is better than watching films at home, because the big screen and the audience make the film more exciting. / On the whole, working from home is more enjoyable because you don't waste time commuting, although you miss your colleagues. / In general, cats make better pets for older people because they tend to be quieter and easier to look after than dogs.

narr: Now let's practice using generalizing language in discussions.
Work in groups of three and take turns discussing the given statements.
First, choose a statement from the list provided.
Then formulate your opinion using the generalizing phrases we've learned.
Provide supporting reasons for your position.
Respond to others' viewpoints using appropriate language.

data.title: Grammar Worksheet
data.subtitle: Present Simple and Adverbs of Frequency

narr: Moving on to grammar exercises focusing on the Present Simple tense and adverbs of frequency.
These exercises will help reinforce the rules we've studied.

data.heading: Exercise 1: Present Simple Form
data.problem:
Complete with the present simple form of the verbs:
1. Sam (not live) near me.
2. Sofia (drive) to work.
3. she (speak) any other languages?
4. I (not like) waking up early.
5. they (see) each other at the weekends?
6. We (be) very tired.
7. Some people (not need) a lot of sleep.
8. (be) your bus late?
9. He (have) a big house in the country.
steps: Identify the subject and required verb form
Apply do/does support for negation and questions
Add -s after he/she/it for third person singular
Use 'has' for have in third person singular
data.result: Answers: (1) doesn't live; (2) drives; (3) Does she speak; (4) don't like; (5) Do they see; (6) are; (7) don't need; (8) Is; (9) has.

narr: Let's begin with Exercise 1, which focuses on forming questions and negatives in the present simple tense.
For each sentence, identify the subject and determine the correct verb form.
Remember to use do/does support for negation and questions.
Add -s after he/she/it for third person singular verbs.
Use 'has' instead of 'have' in the third person singular.
The correct answers demonstrate these rules in action.

data.heading: Exercise 2: Adverb Position
data.problem:
Find and correct five mistakes with the position of frequency adverbs and time expressions:
1. I often am tired at work.
2. We twice a week eat out in a restaurant.
3. Do you often check your phone for messages?
4. She is never late to my lesson.
5. I have two or three times a day a cup of coffee.
6. They don't play often board games.
7. Does usually she take public transport?
steps: Identify the frequency adverbs and time expressions
Check their positions in each sentence
Correct according to rules: adverbs after 'be', after subject in questions, after auxiliary verbs in negatives, frequency expressions at the end
data.result: Sentences 3 and 4 are correct; corrections: (1) I am often tired at work. (adverb after be); (2) We eat out in a restaurant twice a week. (expression of frequency at the end); (5) I have a cup of coffee two or three times a day. (expression at the end); (6) They don't often play board games. (adverb after don't, before the main verb); (7) Does she usually take public transport? (adverb after the subject).

narr: Exercise 2 focuses on the correct positioning of frequency adverbs and time expressions.
First, identify the frequency adverbs and time expressions in each sentence.
Then check their positions according to the rules we've studied.
Remember that adverbs typically come after 'be' verbs.
In questions, they come after the subject but before the main verb.
In negatives, they come after the auxiliary verb but before the main verb.
Frequency expressions usually go at the end of sentences.
Sentences 3 and 4 are already correct, while the others need adjustment.

data.heading: Exercise 3: Complete the Text
data.problem:
Complete the text with words from the boxes:
Box A (frequency words and phrases): always, every day, never, often, rarely, two or three times a month, usually.
Box B (verbs): eat, get up, go, have, leave, make, meet.
The text: I 1 at about 7.30 a.m. and get ready for work. I 3 breakfast because I don't feel hungry in the mornings. I start work at 9 a.m. and at 12 I have a lunch break. I 5 my friend for lunch — normally two or three times a week. At 1.30 I start work again and finish at 5.30 p.m. I like to keep fit, so I 7 to the gym. I get home at about 8.00 p.m. and make dinner, but I also 9 at restaurants 10 . I'm always tired in the evenings so I go to bed early. And that's my day!
steps: Identify gaps requiring frequency words/phrases and verbs
Select appropriate words from Box A and Box B
Apply rules: frequency words before main verbs, frequency phrases at end
Ensure grammatical agreement with subjects and tenses
data.result: Answers: (1) usually +(2) get up; (3) never +(4) have; (5) often +(6) meet; (7) usually +(8) go; (9) eat; (10) two or three times a month. Unused: always, every day, rarely, leave, make.

narr: Finally, Exercise 3 requires completing a text with appropriate frequency words and verbs.
First, identify which gaps need frequency words/phrases and which need verbs.
Then select appropriate words from the provided boxes.
Remember that frequency words typically come before main verbs, while frequency phrases go at the end.
Ensure grammatical agreement with subjects and tenses throughout.
The completed text demonstrates proper use of these elements in context.
